Photograph: Rayhan Ahmed/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock From Afghanistan to Taiwan, unprecedented deluge highlights devastating impact of climate breakdown By Natasha May and Jonathan Watts Tue 28 Jul 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 00.11 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “It rained for 10 days and 10 nights, non-stop – I’d never seen anything like it,” says Anar Gul, a construction worker who lives in the remote district of Dur Baba in eastern Afghanistan . The houses in his village are built from stone and mud, which makes them extremely vulnerable to heavy rains. After days of rain, Gul’s kitchen collapsed and his neighbour, Sayed Afsar Sadat, saw a large part of his house completely destroyed. “Rains like this are coming heavier and earlier each year,” says Sadat. “They are destroying the roads and washing away our crops. It’s impacting us directly.” View image in fullscreen Anar Gul, who lives in a remote mountain village in the Dur Baba district of eastern Afghanistan, says he has never seen rain like it. Photograph: IFRC/Mark South. Last week, torrential rains and flash floods wiped out villages and towns in Afghanistan, leaving at least 31 people dead and hundreds missing. It’s been a similar picture in neighbouring countries, with the monsoon rains sparking chaos across the region. India, Bangladesh and Pakistan have all seen erratic, sudden heavy dumps of water. Jesmin Akter lived in the city of Chattogram, on the south-eastern coast of Bangladesh, which received a record 412.3mm of rainfall in 24 hours in early July, leading to the flash flood that swept through the Banshkhali district where they live. She says her children “understand that we are in a very bad situation”. Overnight the rains took the little they had; their poultry died, their paddy field flooded, their house collapsed and all their belongings in it – children’s books, school bags, toys, clothes, kitchen items – ruined. Akter carried her six children through chest-deep water to her mother’s house. There they stayed in the crowded conditions for over a week until the water receded. View image in fullscreen Residents and rescue workers inspect buildings damaged by heavy flooding in the eastern province of Nuristan, Afghanistan. Photograph: Wahidullah Kakar/AP “We have lost everything,” Akter said. Their house beside the canal was not in a good condition, but a few months ago the family had repaired it. “Now the flood has destroyed it again. We have no money. We are surviving on the food assistance we receive from different organisations.” They have gone back to the ruins of their home, but her children sleep on plastic sheets laid on the wet floor and she worries for their safety, especially that the unsanitary conditions will lead to disease. Her daughter has developed a fever. As wildfires rage across Europe and North America, the unprecedented rains continue elsewhere. While South Korea swings between heatwave and downpour, in Japan and Vietnam torrential rain has led to landslides . China, meanwhile, has seen bouts of extreme rainfall since the flood season began in April, according to the water resources ministry in mid-July, marking the start of a month-long peak flood control window. More than 600 rivers have since risen above warning levels – a 35% jump from the average for the same period over the past five years. View image in fullscreen Sayed Afsar Sadat in Dur Baba says rains are destroying the roads and washing away crops. Photograph: IFRC/Meer Abdullah Rasikh. In the south-western city of Chongqing, a huge landslide after torrential rain killed at least 11 people and left 50 missing, with rescue efforts still ongoing. Separately, a flash flood at a scenic camping spot in the north-central province of Gansu left 10 people dead and injured 23 others. The flood season across the region has been exacerbated by successive storms. Typhoon Noul, the strongest to make landfall in China so far this year, prompted the evacuation of more than 890,000 people in Guangdong as of Sunday evening, according to provincial authorities. In early July, Typhoon Maysak inundated parts of Guangxi and swept through commercial snake farms , allowing hundreds of snakes to escape. Forecasters have warned that more wet weather is on the way. Much of northern China, including Beijing, is expected to receive 20% to 50% more rain than usual, while four to six typhoons are forecast to make landfall in or affect the country this summer, above the average of 4.2, according to the China Meteorological Administration . Taiwan, an island that lies in the path of typhoons in the north-west Pacific, has also seen a rise in extreme rainfall. In June, repeated downpours caused more than NT$330m (about US$10.2m) in agricultural losses across Taiwan, according to the agriculture ministry , while the capital Taipei recorded its highest monthly rainfall in more than a century. View image in fullscreen Torrential rain flooded the streets of Dhaka in Bangladesh. Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters The extreme weather across the region can clearly be linked to climate change. Climate scientists have long predicted that large areas of Asia will disproportionately suffer from more intense heat, humidity and drought as a result of climate disruption caused by the burning of gas, oil and coal. The most recent report by the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change said rising temperatures raise the threat of “floods in monsoon regions in south, south-east and east Asia, and glacier melting in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential Preview latest after newsletter promotion And World Weather Attribution scientists have warned that extreme rainfall from cyclones is being “supercharged” in south-east Asia, with a clear pattern of increasingly heavy rain over recent decades. View image in fullscreen In early July, Typhoon Maysak inundated parts of Guangxi in south China. Photograph: Cao Yiming/Xinhua/AP The year 2025 saw devastating storms and rainfall across the region. It also saw ocean temperatures rise to record heights. So far, this year has brought record-breaking heatwaves . Extreme rainfall is more common and more intense because of human-caused climate breakdown across most of the world, particularly in Europe , most of Asia, central and eastern North America, and parts of South America, Africa and Australia. This is because warmer air can hold more water vapour and flooding has most likely become more frequent and severe in these locations as a result. “More intense rainfall is an expected consequence of us heating the planet by burning fossil fuels and building up more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. A warmer atmosphere can carry more water, so when it rains, it rains harder. Also hotter conditions cause air to rise faster and drive more intense thunderstorms,” said Richard Betts, head of the climate impacts strategic area at the Met Office Hadley Centre. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) in providing aid helped the Guardian obtain interviews with those affected. View image in fullscreen Typhoon Noul (pictured in Hong Kong) prompted the evacuation of more than 890,000 people in Guangdong. Photograph: Venron Yuen/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Dr Hosam Faysal, the head of IFRC’s country delegation in Afghanistan, said “these are the very real, humanitarian effects of a changing climate … becoming increasingly volatile”. Faysal urged governments to ensure there was more investment in locally-led preparedness and mitigation in order to reduce the loss of life and suffering before climate-related disasters happened. “The coming forecast El Niño is a clear example – waiting to respond to the extreme needs we can see coming only once they arrive will cost lives.” Research by Yu-chen Li Explore more on these topics Flooding Asia Pacific Climate crisis China Afghanistan South and central Asia news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty View image in fullscreen A Palestinian flag flown by a protester outside the group’s high court hearing in London in February. Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty Palestine Action US issues sanctions against UK-based direct action group Palestine Action US labels group ‘global terrorist’ as Palestine Action challenge against proscription in UK nears supreme court hearing Haroon Siddique Legal affairs correspondent Wed 26 Aug 2026 13.45 EDT First published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 13.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US ⁠has ​issued sanctions against ⁠the UK-based direct action organisation Palestine ⁠Action, describing it as a “transnational terror group”. The US Department of the Treasury labelled Palestine Action a specially designated global terrorist on Wednesday, which allows the US to freeze the assets of foreign individuals and entities. Palestine Action became the first direct action group to be proscribed under the UK’s Terrorism Act in July last year, placing it alongside the likes of Islamic State and Boko Haram. The UK ban is the subject of a legal challenge that will be heard by the UK supreme court in November. The powers used to sanction the organisation in the US were introduced by President George W Bush shortly after the 9/11 attacks by al-Qaida on the twin towers in New York. Announcing the sanctions on Palestine Action and two other organisations, the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said: “Far-left extremists, their fronts, and their enablers should be on notice: we will bring the full weight of our economic tools to bear. Political terrorism has no place in our society and we will continue to cut the financial lifelines of these groups until they are eliminated.” The co-founder of Palestine Action, Huda Ammori, who is behind the legal challenge to the UK ban, said in response: “Palestine Action’s activities in the US and elsewhere have always been about saving lives by disrupting the Israeli war machine, which is committing a genocide in Gaza with the support of the US government. Trump has been at the centre of the mass murder of Palestinians, enabling the Zionist regime at every turn. View image in fullscreen Huda Ammori, the co-founder of Palestine Action, said the fact that Trump was taking inspiration from Britain’s repression of the movement should be a wake-up call to anyone who cared about civil liberties. Photograph: Abdullah Bailey/Alamy “The fact that Trump is now taking inspiration from Britain’s repression of the movement for Palestinian freedom exposes just how dangerous this ban is and should be a wake-up call to anyone who cares about free speech and civil liberties. By banning a direct action protest group under terrorism legislation for the first time in British history, Keir Starmer’s government has created a blueprint for authoritarian governments around the world to suppress political dissent, and to criminalise British citizens who travel or live abroad. “Trump’s decision to adopt Keir Starmer’s designation of Palestine Action as a ‘terrorist’ group should be the final nail in the coffin of this dangerous, draconian and disproportionate ban.” Palestine Action ban will be overturned, group’s co-founder vows Read more As well as freezing the assets of those sanctioned, the listing forbids US citizens and entities from doing business with them. The US Treasury website said the group had “supported numerous acts of terrorism since July 2020, including acts that have physically injured UK law enforcement personnel, as well as acts intended to intimidate lawful commercial enterprises and coerce the UK government. The group’s actions include multiple high-profile instances of breaking into defense infrastructure and British military installations, and causing millions of dollars’ worth of damage to military equipment.” It said the group had promoted its activities on social media, “encouraging the use of similar tactics internationally, including within the United States and along the US-Mexican border”. In the UK, Palestine Action has focused largely on factories run by the Israeli weapons firm Elbit Systems, as well as other companies that do business with it. In March last year, Donald Trump’s Turnberry golf course on the west coast of Scotland was targeted by protesters . The clubhouse at the five-star resort in Ayrshire was graffitied and the course dug up and painted with the words “Gaza is not 4 sale”. The then UK foreign secretary, Yvette Cooper, moved to ban the group last year after recommendations from officials, who nevertheless conceded that proscribing Palestine Action would be “relatively novel” as “there was no known precedent of an organisation being proscribed on the basis that it was concerned in terrorism mainly due to its use or threat of action involving serious damage to property”. https://www.ksl.com:443/article/51618479.text: KYIV, Ukraine — Four people were killed, and over a dozen injured ​in Russian air attacks on the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv and the surrounding region on Tuesday, local authorities said, in what was the sixth day ‌in a row of strikes on the area.Explosions were heard in Kyiv, a Reuters witness said. Three people were ⁠killed and another five wounded, and a ​fire broke out in a non-residential ⁠area of the capital, city authorities said on the Telegram messaging app.In Boryspil in ‌the Kyiv region, one ‌person was killed and another nine, including a child, were injured after ⁠missiles and drones damaged an apartment building and a ⁠business facility, Governor Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.The attack marks the sixth day of attacks on Kyiv and the surrounding region, disrupting the daily lives of millions of people. Air raid alerts covered most of Ukraine's territory in the early hours of Tuesday.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday he held a "detailed and ‌constructive" call with President Donald Trump's envoys Steve ​Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and that the sides were working to finalize dates for their visit to Ukraine aimed at advancing peace efforts. A firetruck and other vehicles pass by a warehouse hit by a Russian drone strike with a melted Avrora Multimarket sign, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv region, Ukraine, Monday, (Photo: Alina Smutko, Reuters) Moscow shot down over a dozen drones heading in its direction, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram, as Ukraine continues to retaliate on the Russian capital and regions deeper inside the country to force the Kremlin to end its four-and-a-half-year invasion.In Russia's Samara region, ​home to a number of major oil refineries some 800 km (500 miles) southeast of Moscow, an ‌air attack damaged civilian ‌facilities, the ⁠local governor said on Telegram.The NATO Baltic air policing mission has activated jet fighters in Latvia, and Finland has restricted air and maritime traffic close to Russia, armed forces of both countries said separately on X, as Russia's northwestern Leningrad region, home to major ‌export ports, was shooting ​at drones on Tuesday.Russia and Ukraine deny targeting ‌civilians. Reuters could not independently ⁠verify the damage ​reports.

http://insidefutbol.com/2026/09/08/star-.text: Scottish Football > Celtic Star Who Flopped At Celtic Eyed As No-Cost Signing By Polish Side 08/09/2026 - 14:34 BST Shubhansh Singh Ian MacNicol/Getty Images Former Celtic flop Maryan Shved, who is currently on the books of Shakhtar Donetsk, could get the chance to join Jagiellonia Bialystok, who knocked Rangers out of the Europa League, if he terminates his contract with the Ukrainian club. Shved joined Celtic in January 2019 from his boyhood club Karpaty Lviv, but he was immediately loaned back to the Ukrainian club for the remainder of the 2018/19 season. The winger failed to establish himself with the Scottish giants and made only three appearances for Celtic before joining Belgian side KV Mechelen in 2020. Enjoying this story? Add Inside Futbol as a preferred source on Google. He eventually returned to his homeland of Ukraine in 2022 and joined Shakhtar Donetsk, where he has won multiple trophies. The winger has made 54 appearances for the Ukrainian club so far, while scoring nine goals and providing four assists. However, Shved has not been registered for league or cup competitions by Shakhtar Donetsk this season, suggesting he is out of favour at the club. With fresh developments emerging, it appears the former Celtic star could get an option to play in Poland. Season Position 2025–26 1st 2024–25 1st 2023–24 1st 2022–23 1st 2021–22 1st Celtic’s last five league finishes According to Polish outlet Goal.pl , Jagiellonia are willing to sign Shved, but the player would have to terminate his contract with Shakhtar Donetsk before the Polish side make a move for him. Jagiellonia knocked Rangers out in the Europa League playoff round and are keen on signing players with experience, but they want to sign the 29-year-old on a free transfer without any additional fees. With Shved not registered by the Ukrainian side, the winger could look to terminate his contract to secure playing minutes. One former Celtic star moved to Poland earlier this summer, with Luis Palma completing a permanent move to Lech Poznan. Meanwhile, Celtic have made a perfect start to the Scottish Premiership season and sit top of the table after winning all five of their games under Martin O’Neill. O’Neill will want to continue that run on Wednesday evening when Celtic take on St Johnstone at McDiarmid Park. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Anthony Albanese has revealed an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June. The prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York. This incident occurred in June this year and involved an Open AI agent gaining unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia. The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files. A forensic investigation, aided by the Australian Signals Directorate, is now under way to ascertain more information, including what other government systems were affected. The Medicare statistics reporting portal is a public-facing statistics portal that contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending. No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage but investigations are ongoing. Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. No

https://www.dw.com/en/gunmen-kill-27-peo.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NLpK Police are searching for suspects involved in two separate mass shootings in Gauteng and the Western Cape Image: Oupa Nkosi/REUTERS Advertisement At least 27 people have been killed in separate mass shooting incidents in South Africa 's Gauteng and Western Cape provinces overnight. In the first incident, gunmen armed with assault rifles killed 17 people and wounded 15 others at a bar in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg, police said on Sunday. Police say the gunmen shot at patrons outside the bar, then moved inside to continue the killing Image: Oupa Nkosi/REUTERS Manhunt underway for 8 suspects in Wedela shooting Gauteng police said they have launched a manhunt for eight unidentified armed men following the deadly shooting. "They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles," the South African ​Police Service (SAPS) ‌said. Emergency ‌services ‌declared all ​17 victims, 13 men and four women, dead at the scene. Authorities said the shooting occurred Saturday at around 9:30 p.m. local time (1930 UTC). A motive for the shooting ⁠was ​not ​known, the SAPS said, adding that "suspects ​were reportedly ⁠armed with AK-47 rifles ⁠and ​pistols." 10 killed in Lwandle tavern shooting, Cape Town In a separate shooting in the Western Cape, police said gunmen killed 10 people and wounded 11 more at an entertainment venue in Lwandle township at 1:46 a.m. (2346 Saturday GMT). Authorities said five of the victims died at the scene while another five succumbed to their injuries after being taken to hospital. Police said no arrests have been made and that a "multi-disciplinary team" led by serious and violent crime detectives had been established to track down those responsible. More police resources have been sent to the area as the search for the perpetrators continues. Residents in both communities have been left stunned following the shootings Image: Esa Alexander/REUTERS The latest incidents came just days after at least 11 people were gunned down at a home in KwaZulu-Natal Province . That shooting occurred in KwaMakhutha, a township some 30 kilometers (19 miles) south of Durban, the eastern province's largest city. SA deploys troops as organized crime grips communities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Sense of 'shock' following Wedela shooting, says DW correspondent DW correspondent Thuso Khumalo was at the scene in Wedela and said there was a definite of "shock" following the shooting. "People are very worried here," Khumalo said, pointing to the number of community members who were standing near the police cordon. On the question of whether the victims had been specifically targeted, Khumalo said police suspected it was a retaliatory attack involving gangs. "They are saying, one of the victims was already on their list, on their radar, the intelligence radar," Khumalo said, adding that he was being investigated for a previous incident. Police said one of the victims was being sought by police in connection with a previous incident Image: Oupa Nkosi/REUTERS Wedela is situated in an area where there has been a security crackdown on illegal mining involving the deployment of police and soldiers. "The criminals think it's a fashion. They want to make it something which we need to get used to, but that cannot be allowed and tolerated," said deputy provincial police commissioner Major General Fred Kekana. South Africa's high rate of violent crime South Africa is grappling with violent crime and has one of the world's highest murder rates, with around 60 people dying violently in the country each day. In one of the stories that has made international headlines in recent days, Johannesburg police are still trying to track down those responsible for a spate of killings in which the bodies of 10 women have been found in close proximity to one another. Police have identified similarities in some of the killings but said they had not found concrete evidence to suggest the same person or people were responsible. In March, South Africa's leadership deployed troops to hotspots to support police dealing with rampant criminality that President Cyril Ramaphosa has described as one of the biggest challenges facing the country at present.
